Drivel is talk or writing that is so stupid, pointless, or empty that it has no real value whatsoever. It is content that wastes your time and insults your intelligence. Think of it as words that add up to absolutely nothing.
Going Deeper: What Exactly Makes Something "Drivel"?

The word drivel captures a very specific kind of badness. It is not just wrong information, and it is not just boring content. Drivel is content that is foolish and worthless at the same time. It fails on two levels — it has nothing meaningful to say, and it says it in a silly or stupid way.

Think of it this way. If someone writes a long article that turns out to be factually incorrect, you might call it misleading or false. But if someone writes a long article that is vague, rambling, pointless, and says nothing of substance at all — that is drivel. The problem is not that it is wrong. The problem is that it is empty and foolish.

There are a few things that typically make something drivel:

It has no real point. You read or listen to the whole thing and come away with nothing. No idea, no insight, no useful information. The words existed purely to fill space or air time.

It is embarrassingly simple or shallow. It treats the audience as if they have no intelligence, or it comes from a place of very little thought or effort.

It is often long-winded. Drivel tends to go on and on. If someone said something nonsensical in one short sentence, you might just call it "silly." But drivel often involves a lot of worthless words — a whole speech, a whole article, a whole book — that amount to nothing.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is important: drivel is a word of contempt. When you call something drivel, you are not mildly criticising it. You are dismissing it completely — treating it as beneath serious consideration. It carries a strong sense of frustration or scorn. You use it when you feel that your time has been wasted, or when you are annoyed that someone is speaking or writing as though they have something important to say when they clearly do not.

It is a confident, cutting word. Saying "that is drivel" is not a gentle critique. It is a firm rejection.
Real-Life Examples to Lock It In

Example 1: A politician gives a long speech full of grand-sounding words, but when you think about it afterward, he made no actual promises, offered no real solutions, and said nothing of substance. A listener might say: "That entire speech was drivel."

Example 2: A self-help book tells you things like "believe in yourself and great things will happen" and "your only limit is your mind" — page after page of vague, obvious, empty statements dressed up to sound wise. A critic might write: "This book is 300 pages of absolute drivel."

Example 3: A celebrity goes on a talk show and rambles incoherently about their "spiritual energy" and "vibrational frequencies" with no clarity or logic. A viewer might say: "I can't listen to this drivel anymore."

Example 4: Someone writes a long complaint letter that goes round and round in circles, repeating the same vague grievances without any clear argument or point. A reader might think: "I've just wasted ten minutes reading drivel."
How It Differs from Similar Words

There are several words that sound similar to drivel, but each has its own flavour. Understanding the differences will make your grasp of drivel much sharper.

Nonsense is the broadest of these words. Nonsense simply means something that does not make sense or is logically wrong. A mathematical error is nonsense. A wild, impossible claim is nonsense. Drivel is a type of nonsense, but it has the extra quality of being foolish and empty — not just wrong.

Gibberish means words that are completely incoherent and impossible to understand — like a jumble of sounds or words that do not form any recognisable meaning. Gibberish is about incomprehensibility. Drivel, on the other hand, is usually understandable — you can follow the words — you just come to realise that they mean nothing of value.

Waffle (especially in British English) means talking or writing at great length without getting to the point. It focuses more on the length and vagueness of the content. Drivel overlaps with waffle but adds the dimension of foolishness and worthlessness.

Rubbish or garbage (when referring to speech or writing) is a general dismissal, similar to drivel in tone but more casual and less specific. Drivel is more pointed — it specifically suggests empty, stupid content, rather than content that is simply bad in a general sense.

Twaddle and balderdash are older, more old-fashioned words for silly or foolish talk. They mean roughly the same as drivel but sound more archaic and are rarely used in everyday modern speech.

Claptrap refers to showy, insincere language that is designed to impress people rather than inform them — empty but flashy talk, often used to win applause or approval. Drivel does not have to be insincere; it can simply be genuinely thoughtless.

So if you want one sentence to remember the difference: drivel is empty, foolish content that you can understand but gain nothing from — and you say it with scorn.

Drivel works naturally in these patterns:

  • "That was complete drivel." (Dismissing something just said or written)
  • "I can't believe I sat through that drivel." (Expressing frustration at wasted time)
  • "The magazine is full of drivel." (Describing a publication with consistently poor, empty content)
  • "Stop spouting drivel." (Telling someone to stop saying foolish, worthless things)

Notice that drivel is most naturally used with words like "complete," "absolute," "utter," or "pure" in front of it — this is because it is already a strong word, and people like to emphasise their contempt when they use it.

Drivel is foolish, empty, worthless talk or writing — content that sounds like it might mean something but, on reflection, says nothing of any value — and when you call something drivel, you are dismissing it with scorn.
